q: Which property distinguishes a crystalline solid from an amorphous solid?
o: It softens gradually over a range of temperature
It melts sharply at a definite temperature
Its particles have no regular arrangement
It behaves like a supercooled liquid
x: Crystalline solids have a regular, repeating arrangement of particles, so all bonds break at one temperature and they melt sharply. Amorphous solids such as glass soften over a range of temperature.

q: A crystal shows different values of refractive index and electrical conductivity when measured in different directions. This property is called:
x: Anisotropy means physical properties depend on direction, because the arrangement of particles differs along different axes of a crystal. Isotropic substances, such as amorphous solids, have the same properties in all directions.

q: Which pair of substances is isomorphous?
x: Isomorphous substances are different compounds with the same crystal form; NaNO₃ and CaCO₃ both crystallise in the same (rhombohedral) form with the same atomic ratio 1 : 1 : 3. Diamond/graphite and the two sulphurs are allotropes, and calcite/aragonite are two forms of one compound.

q: Calcium carbonate occurs naturally as calcite and as aragonite, which have different crystal forms. This is an example of:
x: Polymorphism is the existence of one compound in more than one crystalline form; CaCO₃ as calcite and aragonite is the textbook example. Isomorphism is the opposite idea: different compounds with the same crystal form.

q: The temperature at which rhombic sulphur changes into monoclinic sulphur, both forms being stable at that temperature, is called its:
x: The temperature at which two crystalline forms of a substance can coexist and one changes into the other is the transition temperature. For sulphur it lies below the melting point, so no liquid is formed.

q: When a crystal is broken, it splits along definite directions to give smooth, flat surfaces. These directions are called:
x: Crystals break along cleavage planes, the planes along which the regular layers of particles are most easily separated. Lattice points and unit cells describe the internal arrangement, not the way the crystal breaks.

q: Which of the following is an amorphous solid?
x: Glass has no long-range regular arrangement of particles and softens over a range of temperature, so it is amorphous. Sodium chloride, diamond and ice are all crystalline.

q: Sodium chloride crystallises from water as cubes, but from a solution containing urea it crystallises as octahedra. This shows a change in the crystal's:
x: The shape in which a crystal usually grows is its habit, and it can change with the conditions of crystallisation. The internal arrangement and lattice energy of NaCl stay the same.

q: Which statement about crystalline solids is NOT correct?
o: They are isotropic, with the same properties in all directions
They have a definite geometric shape
Their particles are arranged in a regular repeating pattern
x: Crystalline solids are anisotropic: properties such as conductivity and refractive index vary with direction. Definite shape, sharp melting point and a regular arrangement are all true of crystals.

q: Solid X melts sharply at one temperature and conducts heat differently along different axes. Solid Y softens over a range of temperature and conducts heat equally in all directions. Which conclusion is correct?
o: X is amorphous and Y is crystalline
Both are crystalline but X is polymorphic
X is crystalline and Y is amorphous
Both are amorphous but Y is isotropic
x: A sharp melting point and anisotropy are both signs of a regular crystal lattice, so X is crystalline. Gradual softening and isotropy are signs of an amorphous solid, so Y is amorphous.

q: The radius ratio of an ionic crystal is defined as:
o: Radius of the cation divided by radius of the anion
Radius of the anion divided by radius of the cation
Sum of the radii of the cation and anion
Difference between the radii of the anion and cation
x: Radius ratio = r(cation)/r(anion). Since cations are usually smaller than anions, the value is normally less than 1, and it decides how many anions can fit around each cation.

q: In zinc sulphide (ZnS) the radius ratio is about 0.40. The coordination number of Zn²⁺ in this crystal is:
x: A radius ratio between 0.225 and 0.414 gives tetrahedral coordination, so each Zn²⁺ is surrounded by 4 S²⁻ ions. A ratio of 0.414–0.732 would give 6, and 0.732 or more would give 8.

q: In a crystal of caesium chloride (CsCl), each Cs⁺ ion is surrounded by how many Cl⁻ ions?
x: Cs⁺ is a large cation, so the radius ratio of CsCl is above 0.732 and each Cs⁺ sits at the centre of a cube of 8 Cl⁻ ions. In NaCl the smaller Na⁺ has only 6 Cl⁻ neighbours.

q: Which statement about the effect of ion size on an ionic crystal is correct?
o: A relatively smaller cation can be surrounded by more anions
The radius ratio has no effect on the coordination number
The coordination number depends only on the mass of the ions
A relatively larger cation can be surrounded by more anions
x: As the cation gets larger compared with the anion, more anions can pack around it before they crowd each other, so the coordination number rises (4 → 6 → 8). Mass of the ions plays no part.

q: The radius of Cs⁺ is 169 pm and that of Cl⁻ is 181 pm. What is the radius ratio of CsCl and the resulting coordination number of Cs⁺?
x: Radius ratio = r(cation)/r(anion) = 169/181 ≈ 0.93. Since this is above 0.732, the cation has 8 nearest anions (cubic coordination); 1.07 comes from dividing the wrong way round.

q: NaCl and CsCl are both 1 : 1 chlorides, yet they have different crystal structures. The main reason is that:
o: Cs⁺ is much larger than Na⁺, giving a larger radius ratio
Cs⁺ carries a higher charge than Na⁺
CsCl is covalent while NaCl is ionic
Cs⁺ is smaller than Na⁺, giving a smaller radius ratio
x: Both cations carry a +1 charge, but Cs⁺ is much larger than Na⁺. Its larger radius ratio allows 8 Cl⁻ neighbours instead of the 6 found around Na⁺.

q: In calcium fluoride (CaF₂), each Ca²⁺ ion is surrounded by 8 F⁻ ions. How many Ca²⁺ ions surround each F⁻ ion?
x: Because of the charges (Ca²⁺ and F⁻), there are twice as many F⁻ ions as Ca²⁺ ions, so the coordination number of F⁻ is half that of Ca²⁺: 8/2 = 4. This shows how ionic charge affects crystal structure.

q: Which of the following is one of the factors that decide the shape of an ionic crystal?
o: The molar mass of the compound
The ratio of the radii of the cation and anion
The boiling point of the compound
x: The geometry of an ionic crystal depends on how the ions can pack, which is decided by factors such as the radius ratio and the charges of the ions. Molar mass, colour and boiling point do not decide the arrangement.

q: An ionic compound MX has a radius ratio of 0.60. The arrangement of anions around each cation is expected to be:
x: A radius ratio between 0.414 and 0.732 gives octahedral coordination with 6 anions around each cation, as in NaCl. Below 0.414 the coordination would be tetrahedral; above 0.732 it would be cubic.

q: In an ionic crystal of formula type MX (equal numbers of cations and anions), the coordination numbers of M and X are:
x: With a 1 : 1 ratio of ions, each cation has as many anion neighbours as each anion has cation neighbours, e.g. 6 : 6 in NaCl and 8 : 8 in CsCl. Unequal ratios arise only in compounds like CaF₂.

q: Which of the following forms a molecular crystal?
x: Solid iodine consists of I₂ molecules held together by weak van der Waals forces, so it is a molecular crystal. NaCl is ionic, diamond is a covalent network and copper is metallic.

q: The particles in a molecular crystal are held together by:
o: Electrostatic forces between oppositely charged ions
Covalent bonds running through the whole crystal
Intermolecular forces such as van der Waals forces and hydrogen bonds
Metallic bonds between positive kernels and free electrons
x: In molecular crystals the units are molecules, attracted by relatively weak intermolecular forces (van der Waals forces, dipole forces or hydrogen bonds). Ionic attraction holds ionic crystals; covalent bonds throughout hold network solids like diamond.

q: Solid sodium chloride does not conduct electricity, but molten sodium chloride does. This is because:
o: The solid contains molecules while the melt contains ions
The ions are fixed in the solid but free to move in the melt
Electrons become free only when the solid melts
The solid has no ions until it is melted
x: NaCl is made of ions in both states. In the solid they are held in fixed lattice positions; on melting they become mobile and can carry current. Conduction is by ions, not free electrons.

q: Ionic crystals are hard but brittle. They shatter when struck because:
o: Their ions are held only by weak van der Waals forces
They contain free electrons that move under stress
Their lattice energies are very low
A slight shift of layers brings like-charged ions together, and their repulsion splits the crystal
x: When a layer of ions is displaced, ions of the same charge come face to face and repel strongly, so the crystal cracks along a plane. The ionic forces themselves are strong, which is why the crystals are hard.

q: Which property is typical of molecular crystals?
o: They are soft and have low melting points
They are very hard and have very high melting points
They are brittle with high lattice energies
x: Weak intermolecular forces make molecular crystals soft, low-melting and often volatile. They contain no ions, so they do not conduct even when molten; high lattice energy and conduction in the melt are features of ionic crystals.

q: In ice, each water molecule is hydrogen-bonded to:
o: Two other water molecules in a straight line
Six other water molecules arranged octahedrally
Four other water molecules arranged tetrahedrally
Eight other water molecules arranged at the corners of a cube
x: Each H₂O molecule in ice forms four hydrogen bonds (two through its H atoms and two through the lone pairs on O), giving a tetrahedral arrangement and an open three-dimensional structure.

q: In a crystal of sodium chloride, the formula NaCl represents:
o: One separate NaCl molecule held together by a shared pair of electrons
The simplest ratio of Na⁺ to Cl⁻ ions in a giant lattice, with no separate molecules
A pair of Na and Cl atoms held to other pairs by van der Waals forces
A neutral NaCl molecule held to its neighbours by hydrogen bonds
x: An ionic crystal is a continuous three-dimensional array of ions; each Na⁺ is surrounded equally by Cl⁻ ions, so no particular pair forms a molecule. The formula only gives the 1 : 1 ratio. Discrete molecules held by intermolecular forces are found in molecular crystals.

q: Solid carbon dioxide (dry ice) is classified as:
x: Dry ice is made of separate CO₂ molecules held by weak van der Waals forces, which is why it sublimes easily at low temperature. It has no ions, no extended network of covalent bonds and no metallic bonding.

q: A shiny dark solid melts at 114 °C, sublimes on gentle warming, dissolves in CCl₄, and does not conduct electricity either as a solid or when molten. It is:
o: An ionic crystal such as potassium iodide
A covalent network crystal such as diamond
A molecular crystal such as iodine
A metallic crystal such as zinc
x: Low melting point, easy sublimation, solubility in a non-polar solvent and no conduction even when molten all point to molecules held by weak forces: iodine. An ionic solid would conduct when molten, and diamond and zinc melt far higher.

q: Which statement correctly compares the melting points of NaCl and I₂?
o: I₂ melts higher because iodine molecules are heavier than NaCl units
NaCl melts much higher because its ionic attractions are far stronger than the van der Waals forces between I₂ molecules
They melt at similar temperatures because both are crystalline
NaCl melts higher because its molecules are held by hydrogen bonds
x: NaCl is an ionic crystal with strong electrostatic forces in every direction, so it melts at about 800 °C. Iodine is a molecular crystal with weak intermolecular forces and melts near 114 °C. NaCl has no molecules or hydrogen bonds.

q: In the sodium chloride crystal, the Cl⁻ ions (and likewise the Na⁺ ions) are arranged in a:
x: NaCl has a face-centred cubic arrangement: each set of ions forms an fcc lattice, and each ion sits at the centre of an octahedron of six oppositely charged ions.

q: The smallest part of a crystal lattice which, when repeated in three dimensions, generates the whole lattice is called the:
x: The unit cell is the smallest repeating unit of a crystal lattice. Lattice points are the positions occupied by particles; habit and cleavage describe the outer shape and breaking of the crystal.

q: How many parameters are needed to describe the size and shape of a unit cell?
x: A unit cell is described by three edge lengths and the three angles between them, six parameters in all. Seven is the number of crystal systems and fourteen the number of Bravais lattices.

q: A unit cell has all three edges equal and all three angles equal to 90°. It belongs to the:
x: Equal edges with all angles 90° define the cubic system (e.g. NaCl). Tetragonal has only two equal edges, orthorhombic has three unequal edges, and rhombohedral has equal edges but angles other than 90°.

q: A unit cell has two equal edges and a third different one; two angles are 90° and the third is 120°. The crystal system is:
x: The hexagonal system has a = b ≠ c with α = β = 90° and γ = 120°. Tetragonal also has two equal edges but all three angles are 90°.

q: Crystals are classified into how many crystal systems?
x: There are seven crystal systems: cubic, tetragonal, orthorhombic, monoclinic, triclinic, hexagonal and rhombohedral. Fourteen is the number of Bravais lattices, not systems.

q: A simple cubic unit cell has one atom at each of its 8 corners and no other atoms. How many atoms belong to one unit cell?
x: Each corner atom is shared by 8 neighbouring unit cells, so it contributes 1/8 to each. 8 × 1/8 = 1 atom per unit cell.

q: A face-centred cubic unit cell has an atom at each of the 8 corners and at the centre of each of the 6 faces. The number of atoms per unit cell is:
x: Corners: 8 × 1/8 = 1; faces: 6 × 1/2 = 3 (each face atom is shared by two cells). Total = 1 + 3 = 4. Fourteen comes from counting every atom as wholly inside the cell.

q: In a cubic unit cell, atoms of element X occupy all the corners and atoms of element Y occupy all the face centres. The simplest formula of the compound is:
x: X: 8 corners × 1/8 = 1 atom; Y: 6 faces × 1/2 = 3 atoms. The ratio X : Y = 1 : 3, so the formula is XY₃. X₈Y₆ ignores the sharing of atoms between cells.

q: A crystal lattice is:
o: A random arrangement of particles in a solid
A regular three-dimensional array of points showing the positions of particles in a crystal
The energy that holds the ions of a crystal together
The outer shape of a single crystal grain
x: A crystal lattice is the orderly, repeating three-dimensional pattern of points (lattice points) at which the particles of a crystal are located. The energy holding ions together is lattice energy, a different idea.

q: Which crystal system has the lowest symmetry, with all three edges unequal and all three angles unequal and none equal to 90°?
x: Triclinic has a ≠ b ≠ c and α ≠ β ≠ γ ≠ 90°, the least symmetric arrangement. Monoclinic still has two angles of 90°, and orthorhombic has all angles 90°.

q: Lattice energy is the energy:
o: Released when one mole of an ionic crystal is formed from its gaseous ions
Released when one mole of an ionic crystal is formed from its elements
Absorbed when one mole of an ionic solid dissolves in water
Released when one mole of gaseous atoms gains electrons
x: Lattice energy refers to gaseous ions coming together to form one mole of the ionic crystal. Formation from the elements is the enthalpy of formation, and electron gain by atoms is electron affinity.

q: Which equation represents the change whose energy is the lattice energy of sodium chloride?
x: Lattice energy concerns gaseous ions forming one mole of solid crystal. The second equation is the enthalpy of formation, the third is dissolving, and the last starts from neutral gaseous atoms, not ions.

q: The magnitude of lattice energy increases when:
o: The charges on the ions increase and their radii decrease
The charges on the ions decrease and their radii increase
The radii of the ions increase, whatever their charges
The molar mass of the compound increases
x: Attraction between ions is stronger for higher charges and shorter distances, so small, highly charged ions give the largest lattice energies. Molar mass by itself does not decide it.

q: Which shows the sodium halides in order of decreasing magnitude of lattice energy?
x: The cation and charges are the same, so lattice energy depends on anion size. F⁻ is smallest and I⁻ largest, so the lattice energy falls from NaF to NaI.

q: For NaCl (kJ mol⁻¹): ΔHf = −411; sublimation of Na = +108; ½ dissociation of Cl₂ = +121; ionisation energy of Na = +496; electron affinity of Cl = −349. Using a Born–Haber cycle, the lattice energy (for Na⁺(g) + Cl⁻(g) → NaCl(s)) is:
x: Lattice energy = ΔHf − (108 + 121 + 496 − 349) = −411 − 376 = −787 kJ mol⁻¹. Taking the electron affinity as +349 instead gives −1485, a common sign mistake.

q: Lattice energy cannot be measured directly. It is usually calculated using:
o: Burning the solid in a bomb calorimeter
The Born–Haber cycle, based on Hess's law
x: The Born–Haber cycle links lattice energy to measurable quantities (enthalpy of formation, sublimation, bond dissociation, ionisation energy, electron affinity) through Hess's law.

q: Magnesium oxide melts at a far higher temperature than sodium chloride. The main reason is that:
o: MgO has a much larger lattice energy because Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ carry double charges
MgO is a covalent compound while NaCl is ionic
NaCl molecules are held together by weak van der Waals forces
Magnesium atoms are heavier than sodium atoms
x: Both are ionic, but the 2+ and 2− charges in MgO (and its small ions) give much stronger attraction, so its lattice energy and melting point are far higher. NaCl contains ions, not molecules.

q: Which compound has the greater lattice energy, and why?
o: KF, because K⁺ is larger than Li⁺
KF, because potassium has more electrons
LiF, because Li⁺ carries a larger charge than K⁺
LiF, because Li⁺ is smaller than K⁺
x: Li⁺ and K⁺ both carry +1, but Li⁺ is much smaller, so the Li⁺–F⁻ distance is shorter and the attraction stronger. A larger ion lowers lattice energy.

q: Which shows MgO, NaCl and KCl in order of decreasing magnitude of lattice energy?
x: MgO is highest because its ions carry 2+ and 2− charges. NaCl and KCl both have +1/−1 ions, but Na⁺ is smaller than K⁺, so NaCl is above KCl.

q: The magnitude of the lattice energy of an ionic compound is a measure of:
o: The strength of the covalent bonds inside each ion
The energy needed just to melt one mole of the solid
The strength of the ionic bonding holding the crystal together
The electron affinity of the anion
x: A large lattice energy means the ions attract each other strongly, so it measures the strength of ionic bonding in the crystal. Melting does not separate the ions into gaseous ions, so it is not the same quantity.
